longQuestions: Estimation is the process of using sample data to obtain values (point or interval) for unknown population parameters.
An estimator is the rule, formula or statistic used to estimate a parameter (x̄ = Σx/n); an estimate is the numerical value obtained by applying the estimator to a particular sample (x̄ = 52.4).
i) Statistical inference — drawing conclusions about a population from sample information; its two branches are estimation and testing of hypotheses.

ii) Types of estimates — point estimate: a single value used as the estimate of the parameter (x̄ = 50); interval estimate: a range of values with a stated confidence that it contains the parameter (48 < μ < 52 with 95% confidence).
i) A point estimate is a single number used as the estimate of a parameter; an interval estimate is a range (L, U) together with a confidence level that it contains the parameter.
ii) An estimator is the formula or statistic (a random variable); an estimate is the particular value of the estimator obtained from a given sample.
i) Unbiasedness — an estimator T is unbiased for θ if E(T) = θ; e.g. x̄ is unbiased for μ and s² = Σ(x−x̄)²/(n−1) is unbiased for σ².
ii) Efficiency — of two unbiased estimators, the one with smaller variance is more efficient; e.g. for a normal population the mean is more efficient than the median.
iii) Consistency — T is consistent if it approaches θ as n increases (its variance tends to 0); x̄ is consistent for μ.
iv) Sufficiency — T is sufficient if it uses all the information in the sample about θ; Σx (or x̄) is sufficient for μ.
Bias is the difference between the expected value of an estimator and the true value of the parameter: Bias = E(T) − θ.

Factors introducing bias: faulty sampling methods (non-random selection), an incomplete or outdated sampling frame, non-response, wrong questions or interviewer influence, deliberate wrong answers, faulty measuring instruments and wrong formulas of estimation.
E(T₁) = (μ + 2μ + μ)/4 = μ and E(T₂) = (μ + μ + μ)/3 = μ, so both T₁ and T₂ are unbiased.
Since Var(T₂) < Var(T₁), T₂ (the sample mean) is the more efficient estimator.

Confidence interval estimation gives a range of values (L, U), computed from sample data, that is expected to contain the unknown parameter with a stated probability (confidence level 1 − α), e.g. x̄ ± z_{α/2}·σ/√n for μ.
A 95% confidence interval means that if many samples were taken and intervals made in the same way, about 95% of them would contain the true parameter.
i) Confidence limits — the lower and upper end points L and U of a confidence interval.
ii) Confidence coefficient — the probability (1 − α) that the interval contains the parameter, e.g. 0.95.
iii) Level of significance (α) — the probability that the interval does not contain the parameter (risk of error), e.g. 0.05.
iv) Precision of a confidence interval — measured by its width; a narrower interval is more precise (precision increases with larger n and smaller σ).
The t-distribution is used instead of Z when the population standard deviation σ is unknown and is estimated by s, and the sample size is small (n < 30), the population being approximately normal.
Then the interval is x̄ ± t_{α/2,(n−1)}·s/√n; for large samples Z can be used even when σ is unknown.
